candidate.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: nursing care that promotes and supports emotional, mental and social well-being during stressful events. Relevant family-focused activity includes assessment of family dynamics to determine the care plan, with psychosocial support, coping, and therapeutic communication integrated into care.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — family-role adjustment and caregiver support after stroke
candidate.educational_objective: Support family adjustment after stroke by acknowledging role changes and caregiver stress, assessing support needs, and linking caregivers with individualized education and community resources.

options.A: Acknowledge the role changes and stress, assess the family's support needs, and connect the caregiver with education and community or respite resources.
options.B: Reassure the spouse that caregiver stress usually resolves once the client is medically stable, so additional support is rarely needed.
options.C: Focus discharge teaching only on the client's physical needs because family adjustment is outside the nursing plan of care.
options.D: Provide one general caregiver handout and avoid follow-up questions so the family can adapt independently.

candidate.rationale: American Stroke Association caregiver guidance notes that stroke can create major role changes and new responsibilities, that caregiving can be stressful and frustrating, and that caregivers may need help from family, community resources, respite services, home health, and stroke support groups. Nursing support should therefore acknowledge the transition, assess needs, provide education, and facilitate appropriate resources. B minimizes caregiver burden, C excludes an important part of psychosocial care, and D substitutes one-time generic information for individualized support.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports acknowledging caregiver role changes and stress and connecting stroke caregivers with individualized education, emotional support, and community/respite resources rather than assuming medical stability eliminates family support needs.
candidate.source_document_title: Let's Talk About Being a Caregiver for a Stroke Survivor
candidate.source_locator: Sections 'What should a stroke caregiver do?' and 'Is there assistance for caregivers?': caregiver responsibilities vary with the survivor's unique needs; role changes and new skills may be needed; caregiving can be stressful and frustrating; caregivers should rely on others when needed; community resources include home health, personal-care support, respite care, meal programs, and stroke support groups for education and emotional support.
candidate.source_organization: American Stroke Association / American Heart Association
candidate.source_version_date: Current American Stroke Association resource accessed 2026-08-18
candidate.stem: A spouse has become the primary caregiver for a client with major functional changes after stroke and says, "I don't know how our family is going to adjust to all of this." Which nursing response is best?
